title: Processes with many steps: state machines and durable workflows
dek: Placing an order means charging a card, telling the restaurant, finding a rider and telling the customer, over minutes and across services. Any step can fail or stall. Here is how to keep such a process in a known state, move it on when nothing happens, and survive a crash halfway through.

items: An order, a payout or a refund is a process whose steps span minutes or days and several services. Any step can fail, and the process must still end somewhere sensible.
Model it as a state machine: each record is in one named state, only listed moves are allowed, and timers move it on when nothing happens.
For long processes with many steps, a workflow engine saves each step's result, so after a crash the process resumes instead of starting over or repeating steps.

body.x: Why one request can't do it all

The simplest way to place an order is one request handler that charges the card, tells the restaurant, finds a rider and tells the customer. If the server dies just after the charge, nobody knows the order exists. If finding a rider takes ten minutes, the request times out long before. A process this long needs its progress written down somewhere that outlives any one server.
One state, a few allowed moves

body.cap: Every order is in one state, and the table of allowed moves rules out the impossible ones, like accepting an order that was already cancelled.

items: Keep the state on the record (`orders.status`) and change it with a conditional update: `SET status = 'accepted' WHERE id = 9051 AND status = 'placed'`. A move that isn't allowed changes no rows.
Keep the table of allowed moves in one place in the code, and record every change with its time and reason. That history answers most support questions.
Timers belong to the design: 'no answer in 5 minutes', 'not picked up in 30'. Store a due time with the state, and let a scheduler pick up overdue records every few seconds.

A move often triggers work, such as a charge, a message or a refund. Save the state change and the message together with an outbox: write the message to an outbox table in the same transaction, and let a separate process send it. The Change data capture concept shows how.

body.cap: The history is what makes the crash harmless. Replaying it tells the new worker which steps are done and what they returned.

body.x: A workflow engine (Temporal, Cadence, or the one your cloud provider offers) runs process code as if crashes didn't happen; the Temporal page in Components goes further. It records the result of every step in a history. When a worker dies, another one replays the history: finished steps hand back their saved results at once, and the code carries on from the first step that hasn't run.

items: Steps still run at least once: a worker can finish a step and die before it is recorded. Make every step idempotent, for example by using the order ID as the payment's idempotency key.
The workflow code must be deterministic, so a replay takes the same path: no reading the clock or random numbers directly. Engines give you their own versions of both.
Waiting is cheap. A workflow can sleep for days, as in 'remind the restaurant in 30 days', without holding a thread.
Undoing is explicit: when step 3 fails for good, run the compensating steps for 2 and 1 in reverse, as in a saga.

body.x: When an engine is too much

Many processes need only the state machine: a status column, the table of allowed moves, a scheduler for timeouts and a queue for the work each move starts. Bring in a workflow engine when processes have many steps, branches and long waits, or when you notice you are writing a scheduler, retries and step history by hand.

items: Draw the states and moves of the main record (order, booking, payment) before drawing the services.
Name the timers: what happens when nobody accepts, nobody pays, nobody picks up.
Say where progress is saved, so a crash resumes the process instead of restarting it.
Make every step safe to run twice, and say how a failed process is undone.

body.label: Go deeper: steps that wait for a person

body.x: Some steps wait for a person: a restaurant approving a refund, a check of a rider's documents. Model each as a state with a deadline and a reminder, such as 'waiting for approval; remind after 4 hours, escalate after 24', not as a request left hanging. The process should always know who it is waiting for, and until when.
